title: Can SAE Features Detect When a Model Is About to Hallucinate?

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Compelling and critical: hallucination detection is a top safety concern. Whether SAE features can serve as mechanistic factuality monitors directly determines a key safety application of interpretability.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Requires curating a verified correct/hallucination dataset (300 questions, 10 samples each for verification), training logistic regression on SAE features, and comparing baselines. Intermediate for beginners.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Dataset curation (verifying 300 questions via sampling) plus classifier training plus held-out evaluation is substantial. Sustained effort for 30 hours.

novelty.reasoning: This idea has been largely addressed by multiple recent works. The ICLR 2025 paper identifies SAE latents that distinguish known/unknown entities as hallucination indicators. The SAFE framework and LVLM steering work both use SAE features to detect and mitigate hallucinations. The core research question—whether SAE features can detect impending hallucination—has been answered affirmatively with working implementations.

evidence.source: Steering LVLMs via SAE for Hallucination Mitigation (arXiv 2505.16146, 2025)
evidence.finding: Uses SAEs to identify semantic directions correlated with hallucinatory content and steers models away from hallucination using SAE latents.

evidence.source: SAFE: SAE-Based Framework for Hallucination Mitigation (arXiv 2503.03032, 2025)
evidence.finding: SAFE uses SAE-driven query enrichment to identify and suppress hallucination-prone features in LLMs via entropy-based uncertainty assessment.
SAE latents in the final token of entity residual stream can distinguish known vs unknown entities, providing a mechanism for detecting when models might hallucinate.
